question.prompt: The measures of the smallest angles of three different right triangles sum to \(90^\circ.\) All three triangles have side lengths that are primitive Pythagorean triples. Two of them are \(3\)-\(4\)-\(5\) and \(5\)-\(12\)-\(13.\) What is the perimeter of the third triangle?

solutions.title: Add the known angles
solutions.explanation:
The tangent of a right triangle's smallest angle is its shorter leg divided by its longer leg, so the two given triples provide exact angle information.

Let \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) be the smallest angles of the three triangles, respectively. Then
\[
\tan\alpha=\frac34,\qquad \tan\beta=\frac5{12}.
\]
Using the tangent addition formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tan(\alpha+\beta)
&=\frac{\tan\alpha+\tan\beta}{1-\tan\alpha\tan\beta}\\
&=\frac{\frac34+\frac5{12}}{1-\frac34\cdot\frac5{12}}
=\frac{56}{33}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\gamma=90^\circ-(\alpha+\beta)\), its tangent is the reciprocal:
\[
\tan\gamma=\frac{33}{56}.
\]
Thus the third triangle's shorter and longer legs are in the ratio \(33:56\). The corresponding hypotenuse is
\[
\sqrt{33^2+56^2}=\sqrt{4225}=65.
\]
Because \(33\) and \(56\) have no common factor greater than \(1\), every integer triangle with this leg ratio has sides \(33k,56k,65k\) for a positive integer \(k\). The requirement that the triple be primitive forces \(k=1\).

The perimeter is therefore
\[
33+56+65=\boxed{154},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Build the angle sum geometrically
solutions.explanation:
We can build the sum of the two known angles by joining scaled copies of the given right triangles. Coordinates then reveal the third triangle's sides without an angle-addition formula.

Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be the smallest angles of the \(3\)-\(4\)-\(5\) and \(5\)-\(12\)-\(13\) triangles. Place
\[
O=(0,0),\qquad P=(48,0),\qquad Q=(48,20).
\]
Triangle \(OPQ\) is a \(5\)-\(12\)-\(13\) triangle scaled by \(4\), so \(OQ=52\) and \(\angle POQ=\beta\).

At \(Q\), draw \(QS\perp OQ\), choosing \(S\) on the opposite side of line \(OQ\) from \(P\), and set \(QS=39\). Triangle \(OQS\) is a \(3\)-\(4\)-\(5\) triangle scaled by \(13\), since its perpendicular legs are \(39\) and \(52\). Hence \(OS=65\) and \(\angle QOS=\alpha\).

To find \(S\), turn the displacement \((48,20)\) through \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise. Its horizontal and vertical components become \((-20,48)\). This displacement has length \(52\); multiplying it by \(39/52=3/4\) gives the displacement from \(Q\) to \(S\):
\[
\frac34(-20,48)=(-15,36).
\]
Therefore
\[
S=(48,20)+(-15,36)=(33,56).
\]
Let \(X=(33,0)\). Triangle \(OXS\) is right at \(X\), with sides \(33,56,65\). Its angle at \(O\) is \(\alpha+\beta\), so its angle at \(S\) is
\[
90^\circ-(\alpha+\beta),
\]
the required third smallest angle. It is indeed the smaller acute angle because its opposite leg is \(33<56\).

Since \(\gcd(33,56)=1\), this triangle is primitive. Any other integer triangle with the same angles is an integer multiple of it, so the primitive condition selects these exact lengths. The perimeter is
\[
33+56+65=\boxed{154},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
